questions.s: Intrinsic fibres arising from the facial motor nucleus:
o: Loop around the abducent nucleus forming the internal genu
The genu and abducent nucleus together raise the facial colliculus.
Pass through the red nucleus
That is the oculomotor nerve.
Leave the brainstem through the inferior cerebellar peduncle
They emerge at the lower border of the pons, above the olive.
Arise from a nucleus lying in the floor of the fourth ventricle directly beneath the colliculus
Last's: the facial nucleus lies deep in the reticular formation of the lower pons. The abducent nucleus, not the facial nucleus, lies beneath the colliculus.
The superior rectus subnucleus supplies the contralateral superior rectus
Its fibres cross, so a nuclear lesion causes bilateral superior rectus weakness.
Each levator palpebrae is supplied from its own side only
Levator is supplied from a single midline central caudal subnucleus to both sides, so nuclear lesions give bilateral ptosis.
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus lies caudal to the somatic nucleus
Last's: it lies cranial (rostral) to the somatic part.
A unilateral nuclear lesion can produce isolated unilateral ptosis
Because levator is supplied from a single midline subnucleus, ptosis from a nuclear lesion is bilateral.

questions.s: A right trochlear nucleus lesion produces:
o: Weakness of the right superior oblique
Trochlear fibres decussate, so the right nucleus supplies the left superior oblique.
Weakness of the left superior oblique
Last's: each trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique of the opposite side.
Head tilt towards the left
Patients tilt the head away from the side of the weak superior oblique, i.e. towards the right here.
Vertical diplopia worse on looking down and to the right
The left superior oblique depresses the adducted left eye, which occurs on looking down and right.

questions.s: Regarding the abducent nerve in the posterior fossa and petrous apex:
o: It runs upward between the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and the pons
Last's: in the pontine cistern.
It pierces the dura on the clivus above the level of the jugular tubercle
True. After running up through the pontine cistern, VI pierces the dura on the clivus above the jugular tubercle and runs between the dural layers to the petrous apex. (Last's)
It enters the cavernous sinus through the inferior petrosal sinus beneath the petroclinoid ligament
Dorello's canal.
It enters the tendinous ring above the superior division of the oculomotor nerve
Last's: it enters below the inferior division of III.

questions.s: Concerning the trigeminal nerve root and Meckel's cave:
o: In Meckel's cave the mandibular fibres lie most laterally and the ophthalmic most medially
Last's: at the pons the mandibular fibres are superior and ophthalmic inferior; the root then rotates.
The motor root emerges above and medial to the sensory root
Last's. It spirals to enter the cave below the sensory root.
The cave contains CSF around the posterior half of the ganglion
Last's: the dura fuses with the pia halfway along the ganglion.
The ganglion's chief blood supply is the posterior communicating artery
Last's: ganglionic branches of the ICA and, appreciably, the accessory meningeal artery.

questions.s: An extradural middle fossa approach to the trigeminal ganglion:
o: Is possible because the anterior ganglion and mandibular division lie between two layers of dura
True. The anterior half of the ganglion and the mandibular division lie between the dural layers of the middle fossa floor, so stripping the dura reaches them without entering the CSF. (Last's)
May cause transient facial palsy from traction on the greater petrosal nerve
Last's: oedema at the geniculate ganglion compresses facial motor fibres.
Necessarily enters the subarachnoid space to reach the sensory root
The sensory root and posterior half of the ganglion are bathed in CSF, but the extradural approach to the anterior ganglion avoids the subarachnoid space.
Risks the abducent nerve less than the trochlear nerve because the abducent lies in the lateral sinus wall
VI lies within the sinus, not in its lateral wall.
The glossopharyngeal nerve lies lateral to the inferior petrosal sinus in the anterior compartment
True. In the anterior compartment IX lies lateral to the inferior petrosal sinus, separated from X and XI by a fibrous septum. (Last's)
The vagus lies lateral to the accessory nerve
Last's: the accessory lies lateral to the vagus in the middle compartment.
The cochlear canaliculus opens into the glossopharyngeal notch
Last's: perilymph drains to the subarachnoid space here.
The jugular bulb occupies the posterior and largest compartment
True. The sigmoid sinus expands into the jugular bulb in the posterior and largest compartment, then becomes the IJV. (Last's)

questions.s: Concerning the vagus and cranial accessory nerve:
o: The superior vagal ganglion contains cell bodies for the meningeal and auricular branches
True. The small superior ganglion holds cell bodies only for the meningeal and auricular branches; the inferior ganglion holds all the other vagal afferents. (Last's)
The inferior vagal ganglion contains cell bodies of the other vagal sensory fibres
Including laryngeal, cardiac and visceral afferents.
The cranial accessory fibres join the vagus at the inferior vagal ganglion
Last's: they are effectively the vagal motor root from the nucleus ambiguus.
The spinal accessory rootlets emerge anterior to the denticulate ligament
Last's: they emerge from the lateral cord behind the denticulate ligament.
Its rootlets pass through the inferior olivary nucleus before emerging
True. Hypoglossal fibres pass ventrally through the inferior olivary nucleus and emerge between pyramid and olive. (Last's)
All its non-lingual branches carry C1 fibres
Meningeal, superior root of ansa, thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.
It exits the skull medial and posterior to the jugular foramen
Last's: the hypoglossal canal lies deep to the jugular foramen.
It supplies all the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue
Palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.s: Concerning the arterial supply and relations of the optic pathway (Last's):
o: The optic tract is supplied chiefly by the anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries
True. The anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries supply the optic tract. (Last's)
The chiasma and intracranial optic nerve are supplied by the anterior cerebral artery
True. The chiasma and the intracranial optic nerve are supplied by branches of the anterior cerebral artery. (Last's)
A pituitary tumour first compresses the upper posterior part of the chiasma
Last's: it presses on the lower anterior part of the chiasma and the medial sides of the optic nerves.
The central retinal artery supplies about the anterior 1 cm of the intraorbital nerve
Last's: the posterior 2 cm by the ophthalmic artery.

questions.s: According to Last's, the approximate numbers of fibres in cranial nerves are:
o: Oculomotor about 24 000
True. The oculomotor nerve has about 24 000 fibres; the trochlear is the smallest with about 3400. (Last's)
Trochlear about 34 000
About 3400; it is the smallest cranial nerve.
Abducent about 6600
True. The abducent nerve contains about 6600 fibres. (Last's)
Cochlear about 3000
About 30 000. The vestibular nerve has about 18 000.

questions.s: On the base of the skull:
o: Foramen rotundum lies anteromedial to foramen ovale
Foramen rotundum lies in front of and slightly medial to foramen ovale, opening into the pterygopalatine fossa.
The carotid canal opens posterior to foramen ovale
The carotid canal lies posteromedial to foramen ovale and spinosum, in the petrous bone.
Foramen spinosum lies anteromedial to foramen ovale
Foramen spinosum lies posterolateral to foramen ovale.
The petrosal foramen, when present, lies behind foramen ovale and transmits the lesser petrosal nerve
Last's. The venous foramen of Vesalius lies medial to it.
